Three contemporary Western writers urge conservatives toward rule by one man or by one confession.

**Stephen Wolfe** (*The Case for Christian Nationalism*, 2022) rightly notes that human beings are particular and need cultural continuity (Principle 4). He then proposes a Christian prince, envisioning "a measured and theocratic Caesarism." He writes that the civil magistrate "can punish external religion," naming "heretical teaching, false rites, blasphemy, and Sabbath-breaking," though not belief itself. Non-Christians, he writes, "are entitled to justice, peace, and safety, but they are not entitled to political equality." In a 2023 interview he held it "permissible in principle to execute arch-heretics." A magistrate who holds the sword against heretical teaching must decide which teaching is heretical, and under Principle 2 he decides as a limited and self-interested man. European history from 1524 to 1648 shows where that leads. The Thirty Years' War (1618 to 1648) alone cost the Holy Roman Empire about five million lives, counting deaths from disease, a fifth of its population before the war (Peter H. Wilson, *The Thirty Years War: Europe's Tragedy*, 2009). That history is why American Christians established the constitutional separation of church and state. A magistrate given the sword to enforce theology corrupts the church and persecutes his fellow Christians over which confession is orthodox.

**Curtis Yarvin** (*Patchwork*, 2008, and later essays) rightly diagnoses how unaccountable administrative bureaucracies and media-academic complexes ("the Cathedral") subvert democratic accountability. His remedy is a realm "governed by its own joint-stock corporation without regard to the residents' opinions." He calls himself "an absolute monarchist," calls the separation of powers a "bogus political panacea," and holds that "no sovereign can be subject to law." In 2024 he wrote that an American executive will not work until the President "considers both the judicial and legislative branches purely ceremonial and advisory." He grants the danger that Principle 2 names: "even the best king can develop a brain tumor, go insane, and order the extermination of the Irish." His answer is that the shareholders may dismiss the chief executive. That check is held by the owners, whose interest is the return on the realm. The residents, who bear the ruler's errors, hold no check at all: "The design is all 'exit,' no 'voice.'" Under Principle 2 the owners are as limited and self-interested as the ruler they appoint.

**Charles Haywood** ("The Foundationalist Manifesto," 2021) proposes a government that "will not be democratic." It "could be Augustan," he writes, "a limited dictatorship (and almost certainly will be to begin)," and "In pursuit of its limited ends, it will have unlimited means." He looks for a Caesar, "a sovereign dictator, who channels the constituent power of the nation to create something that did not exist before, with a fresh constitution." Haywood praises the rule of law elsewhere, but he expects that under Caesar "the rule of law is likely to bend, if not break at some places and times," and that Caesar "will, at least sometimes, therefore resort to proscription and extra-legal action." His advice for the day Caesar comes is to "celebrate." Proscription is a penalty decided after the fact against named persons. It fails Principle 5, which requires rules known beforehand and applied alike. Under Principle 2, the man trusted to bend the law for a good end is limited and self-interested, and once the law bends, the citizens have no procedure to stop him when his ends change.

When Jesus's core moral instructions are read within their actual jurisdictional scope, their alignment with the Five Principles is clear.

Consider first **the Golden Rule** (Matthew 7:12): *"In everything, treat others as you would want them to treat you, for this fulfills the law and the prophets."* The structure of that precept is direct: before you act toward another person or judge his case, exchange your position with his and ask whether you would accept the same procedure applied to yourself. That is Procedural Symmetry stated in a single sentence that a seven-year-old child can remember for life.

Next is **the beam in your own eye** (Matthew 7:3–5): *"Why do you see the speck in your brother's eye, but fail to see the beam of wood in your own?... First remove the beam from your own eye, and then you can see clearly to remove the speck from your brother's eye."* The order of responsibility is explicit: Self-Anchored, Tiered Ownership (Principle 4 and Virtue 2). Do not begin by policing your neighbor's minor fault while your own household is disordered by a major defect of your own; correct Tier 1 first, *and then* you will possess the clear judgment and moral standing to assist Tier 3.

Third is the pairing of **"Do not judge"** (Matthew 7:1–2) with **"You will recognize them by their fruit"** (Matthew 7:15–20). In modern arguments, whenever one points out that a behavior or ideology is destructive, an opponent frequently quotes the opening words of Matthew 7:1 (*"Do not judge"*) as though Jesus were teaching indiscriminate non-judgmentalism. Read the immediately following sentence (Matthew 7:2): *"For by the standard you judge you will be judged, and the measure you use will be the measure you receive."* And read further on in the same discourse (Matthew 7:15–16): *"Watch out for false prophets, who come to you in sheep's clothing but inwardly are voracious wolves. You will recognize them by their fruit. Grapes are not gathered from thorns or figs from thistles, are they?"* How can anyone distinguish a sheep from a wolf in sheep's clothing, or a fig tree from a thornbush, without exercising **discriminating judgment**? One cannot. Jesus is not forbidding truthful moral and empirical judgment; he is forbidding **hypocritical, asymmetrical judgment** (applying one standard of measure to oneself and a different standard to one's neighbor) and commanding his followers to evaluate teachers and doctrines by their observable consequences in reality (Principles 1, 3, and 5).

Fourth is **"Turn the other cheek"** (Matthew 5:39), which separates personal insult from public defense. When Jesus says in the Sermon on the Mount, *"whoever strikes you on the right cheek, turn the other to him as well,"* the concrete physical detail defines the scope. For a right-handed person facing you to strike your *right* cheek, he must use the **back of his hand**. In first-century Jewish and Roman law, that blow was not a lethal assault, but a formal gesture of **personal insult** intended to provoke a private brawl or duel. Properly scoped, Jesus is teaching personal self-command and refusal to escalate personal insults into private blood feuds. He is *never* commanding a father to stand idle while a murderer kills his children, nor commanding a magistrate or soldier to disband the civil police and armed forces. That is why the New Testament explicitly affirms the tiered duty to provide for and protect one's own family (*"if someone does not provide for his own, especially his own family, he has denied the faith and is worse than an unbeliever,"* 1 Timothy 5:8, Principle 4) and the magistrate's duty to wield lethal force against criminals and enemies (*"it is God's servant for your well-being... government does not bear the sword for nothing. It is God's servant to administer punishment on the person who does wrong,"* Romans 13:4, Principles 4 and 5).

If a socialist government nationalizes the Venezuelan petroleum industry and, for two years while oil prices are high, distributes subsidized consumer goods, the partisan declares: *"Socialism succeeds; credit that outcome to Socialism."*

Three years later, when the unmaintained oil equipment fails, the currency collapses in runaway inflation, and families suffer severe food shortages, one points to the same country and the same government, and the partisan replies: *"That is not the fault of Socialism; it resulted from foreign sabotage, hoarders, adverse weather, and an imperfect implementation of Socialism."*

The structural defect in that reasoning is evident: it applies asymmetrical accounting to historical outcomes. Every favorable result is credited to the theory, while every severe failure caused by executing the theory's own program is attributed to external interference. Three steps detect the defect.

**First, state the program in advance.** What concrete policies does the system prescribe (e.g., abolishing private property, reducing police enforcement, removing examination standards)? Principle 2 gives the reason. People find what they expect to find. The N-rays were falsely claimed in this way. A French physicist announced them in 1903, and only some observers could see them. In 1904 R. W. Wood visited the laboratory and found that the observer could not say when a hand entered the path of the rays or which way a prism was turned, and that a piece of wood in place of a steel file changed nothing (Wood, *Nature* 70, 1904, pp. 530 and 531). A test fixed after the result is fixed by what the observer expects. A program stated after its years is stated to fit them. Ask the partisan what the program is before its years are counted.

**Second, apply the same standard of evaluation to arguments for and against.** This is procedural symmetry, and Principle 5 requires it. The partisan's excuse is a statement like any other. *"foreign sabotage, hoarders, adverse weather"* can be asked who did what, and when, and what it changed. A claim made for the doctrine is asked the same questions. If the successes are counted on the doctrine's word and the failures are excused on the partisan's word, two standards have been applied.

**Third, specify what observable fact would falsify the claim.** Ask directly: *"What concrete outcome in the physical world over the next five years would demonstrate to you that this policy is erroneous?"* Principle 1 gives the reason. Truth is correspondence to reality. A claim that no possible observation could prove false corresponds to none in particular. A small group of Americans once expected a flood on 21 December and a flying saucer to carry them away before it. The fact was named in advance, and it was specific. *"Midnight had passed and nothing had happened."* At about 4:45 in the morning the group received a message: *"The little group, sitting all night long, had spread so much light that God had saved the world from destruction"* (Festinger, Riecken, and Schachter, *When Prophecy Fails*, 1956, p. 68). The believers did not give up the belief. They changed the claim. The flood had been called off, they said, and the new claim stated nothing that an event could show to be false. A claim that fails its test does not cross to the metaphysical side afterward (Chapter 3). If the partisan cannot state a single falsifying condition, he is not conducting empirical inquiry or policy analysis; he is reciting an unfalsifiable dogma (**violating Principle 1**).

Claims about reality are always testable against reality. A doctrine is tested by all of its results, the losses as well as the gains. The three steps are that test: the program, the standard, and the fact that would count against it. By Principle 5, the speaker runs his own doctrine through the same three steps before he requires them of another.

Related to asymmetrical accounting is the familiar "That was not authentic doctrine" evasion (*"The Soviet Union was not real Communism,"* *"The Inquisition was not real Christianity,"* *"Al-Qaeda is not real Islam"*). The defender removes every failed case from the ledger by denying that the people who produced it practiced the doctrine.

How does scoped procedural symmetry distinguish when *"That was not authentic doctrine"* is a **valid boundary distinction** versus when it is a **fallacious evasion**?

The guide is correspondence to reality. The test compares what the actors did with what the doctrine's own texts instruct, and it starts with the scope of the doctrine.

A doctrine that prescribes a political and social order is tested by its program. When rulers carry out what its texts instruct, their conduct corresponds to the doctrine, and the years that follow belong on the doctrine's ledger.

Lenin, Stalin, Mao, and Pol Pot followed Karl Marx's explicit command in the *Communist Manifesto* to *"abolish private property"* and concentrate all credit, transport, agriculture, and manufacturing in a central state monopoly. One cannot rightly claim afterward, "That was not authentic Marxism." The famine was not a departure from the doctrine; the famine was the direct consequence of executing those instructions in the physical world.

An ethic that explicitly leaves politics to another authority has no program to compare with a government's acts. The Gospels are the clearest case. Jesus says, *"give to Caesar the things that are Caesar's, and to God the things that are God's"* (Matthew 22:21), and, *"My kingdom is not from this world"* (John 18:36). Men who bear that religion's name later held power and used it, as the Inquisition did. Their conduct cannot be read off the doctrine. The question is then whether the political act was a direct result of the doctrine. It was, if the doctrine's texts command the act, or if rules that the doctrine's own recognized authorities derive from those texts command it. It was not, if no text commands it and the texts forbid it. An act of the second kind belongs to the men who performed it and not to the doctrine they named.

A written rule of law is the simplest case, because its scope and its text are both explicit. Suppose a corrupt judge accepts a ten-thousand-dollar bribe to alter a verdict in an American courtroom. An American may legitimately state, *"That judge was violating American constitutional law."* Article II, Section 4 of the Constitution makes bribery a ground for removal from office, 18 U.S.C. § 201 makes it a crime, and the judicial oath binds the judge to administer justice without respect to persons (28 U.S.C. § 453).

Principle 5 requires the same test for every doctrine: the accuser's own, the defender's own, and the doctrine under examination alike.
